target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is a productive use of already-dead animals and fetal-pig byproducts
objection: Typical dissection specimens are not just already-dead byproducts: AG2 argues that about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, so classroom dissection contributes to wild capture, local population decline, and reduced biodiversity.

target: AG1’s assumption that schools can justify dissection because the animals are dead byproducts and the practice is educational
objection: Animal dissection is not required to meet major educational standards or medical-training goals, because AP Biology and Next Generation Science Standards do not require it and U.S./Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training.

target: AG1’s claim that real animal dissection is necessary because it provides learning that alternatives cannot match
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations can teach dissection-related anatomy at least as well as, or better than, real dead animals, so students can get the same educational benefit without using animals.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection generally causes wild-capture pressure and biodiversity harm
objection: For the usual school specimens, such as fetal pigs, animals are already dead meat-industry byproducts rather than animals killed or captured for class, so classroom dissection does not itself create new death or capture pressure beyond the food system.

target: AG2’s assumption that models and simulations can fully replace real dissection
objection: Real dissection requires tactile manipulation of actual tissue and real three-dimensional anatomical relationships such as texture, density, and spatial arrangement, which models and simulations do not fully reproduce, so they cannot reliably deliver the same learning outcome.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection lacks unique educational value
objection: Hands-on dissection provides substantial biology-learning benefits, including better understanding of structure and function and improved practical lab competence, so alternatives are unlikely to match its educational value.

target: AG1’s claim that using byproducts avoids broader harms
objection: The byproduct-only account does not match typical practice, because AG2 says about 99% of dissection animals are actually sourced from the wild rather than being already-dead meat-industry byproducts.

target: AG1’s inference that dissection is harmless if it uses byproducts
objection: Because wild-catching dissection animals decreases local populations and biodiversity, typical classroom dissection still produces significant inhumane and environmental harms beyond the fate of any one animal.

target: AG2’s claim that school dissection predictably causes biodiversity harm through wild capture
objection: If schools use animals that are already dead rather than animals captured or killed specifically for class, then classroom dissection does not directly cause the population or biodiversity harms AG2 attributes to it.

target: AG1’s claim that requiring dissection is acceptable because the animals were already dead
objection: Even if animals are already dead, forcing students to physically cut up animal bodies can cause moral and psychological distress for students who object to participating in animal harm, so requiring dissection still imposes avoidable harm on some students.

target: AG2’s claim that requiring dissection forces students to participate in animal harm
objection: If the specimens are already dead and not killed or captured for the lesson, then students are not being required to participate in killing or capturing animals, so AG2’s “avoidable participation in animal harm” objection does not really apply.

target: AG2’s claim that alternative activities make dissection unnecessary
objection: Dissection has unique educational benefits—fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, critical thinking, and science motivation through “aha moments”—that alternatives cannot fully replicate, so it remains educationally valuable.

target: AG1’s reliance on AP Biology, NGSS, and medical training as if they justify dissection
objection: AP Biology and Next Generation Science Standards do not require animal dissection, and U.S. and Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training, so those institutions do not support the claim that dissection is necessary.

target: AG1’s assumption that already-dead specimens make dissection morally acceptable
objection: Even if some specimens are already dead, animal dissection still involves serious inhumane treatment, and that makes it inappropriate to require when it is not needed for learning goals or medical training.

target: AG1’s claim that byproduct specimens avoid extra harm
objection: If schools continue to include dissection in the curriculum, they create additional demand for specimens, and those specimens must be obtained through slaughter, harvesting, or capture somewhere in the supply chain, so dissection still generates unnecessary animal harm.

For common dissection animals like fetal pigs, the specimens are meat-industry byproducts already produced for the food system and otherwise destined for disposal, so classroom use does not require extra killing or capture beyond what already occurs.

target: AG2’s claim that more specimen demand means more animal slaughter/capture
objection: Because over 98% of dissected animals are already dead before the classroom activity, typical school dissection does not actually follow AG2’s chain from classroom demand to increased slaughter or capture in the way claimed.
